claim: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) causes mortality and disability worldwide.
source: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) causes mortality and disability worldwide.
evidence: This is a general statement about TBI that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: TBI can initiate acute cell death followed by secondary injury induced by microglial activation, oxidative stress, inflammation and autophagy in brain tissue.
source: It can initiate acute cell death followed by secondary injury induced by microglial activation, oxidative stress, inflammation and autophagy in brain tissue, resulting in cognitive and behavioral deficits.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about TBI pathophysiology.

claim: TBI results in cognitive and behavioral deficits.
source: It can initiate acute cell death followed by secondary injury induced by microglial activation, oxidative stress, inflammation and autophagy in brain tissue, resulting in cognitive and behavioral deficits.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about TBI outcomes.

claim: Both DP and Pom significantly reduced the injury contusion volume at 24 hr and 7 days.
source: Both agents significantly reduced the injury contusion volume and degenerating neuron number evaluated histochemically and by MRI at 24 hr and 7 days, with a therapeutic window of 5 hr post-injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including histochemical analysis and MRI imaging.

claim: Both DP and Pom significantly reduced degenerating neuron number at 24 hr and 7 days.
source: Both agents significantly reduced the injury contusion volume and degenerating neuron number evaluated histochemically and by MRI at 24 hr and 7 days, with a therapeutic window of 5 hr post-injury.
evidence: This is supported by histochemical and MRI data presented in the study.

claim: DP and Pom have a therapeutic window of 5 hr post-injury.
source: Both agents significantly reduced the injury contusion volume and degenerating neuron number evaluated histochemically and by MRI at 24 hr and 7 days, with a therapeutic window of 5 hr post-injury.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing efficacy at 5 hr but not 7 hr post-injury.

claim: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation were suppressed by DP and Pom.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on microglial markers presented in the manuscript.

claim: TBI-induced astrogliosis was suppressed by DP and Pom.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by GFAP staining data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TBI-induced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines was suppressed by DP and Pom.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by mRNA and protein expression data for cytokines presented in the manuscript.

claim: TBI-induced expression of iNOS was suppressed by DP and Pom.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by iNOS mRNA expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TBI-induced expression of COX-2 was suppressed by DP and Pom.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by COX-2 mRNA and protein expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TBI-induced expression of autophagy-associated proteins was suppressed by DP and Pom.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by p62 and LC3-II protein expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: DP and Pom treatment led to an amelioration of behavioral deficits.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data including EBST, beam walking, mNSS, and tactile tests.

claim: DP provided greater efficacy than Pom in ameliorating TBI-induced deficits.
source: TBI-induced upregulated markers of microglial activation, astrogliosis and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, iNOS, COX-2, and autophagy-associated proteins were suppressed, leading to an amelioration of behavioral deficits with DP providing greater efficacy.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data across multiple measures showing superior performance of DP versus Pom.

claim: DP and Pom mediated reductions in markers of neuroinflammation in animal and cellular studies.
source: Complementary animal and cellular studies demonstrated DP and Pom mediated reductions in markers of neuroinflammation and α-synuclein-induced toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by data from both in vivo TBI studies and in vitro RAW 264.7 cell studies.

claim: DP and Pom mediated reductions in α-synuclein-induced toxicity in cellular studies.
source: Complementary animal and cellular studies demonstrated DP and Pom mediated reductions in markers of neuroinflammation and α-synuclein-induced toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by data from primary dopaminergic neuron cultures challenged with α-synuclein.

claim: Annually, an excess of 10 million people suffer a TBI event worldwide.
source: Annually, an excess of 10 million people suffer a TBI event worldwide (Hyder et al., 2007; Ruff and Riechers, 2012), with some 1.6 to 3.8 million cases occurring within the US alone (Mckee and Daneshvar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some 1.6 to 3.8 million TBI cases occur within the US alone annually.
source: Annually, an excess of 10 million people suffer a TBI event worldwide (Hyder et al., 2007; Ruff and Riechers, 2012), with some 1.6 to 3.8 million cases occurring within the US alone (Mckee and Daneshvar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The majority of TBIs are mild to moderate in character and account for 80–95% of cases.
source: By far the majority of TBIs are mild to moderate in character and account for 80–95% of cases, with severe TBI comprising the balance (LoBue et al., 2019; Tagliaferri et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TBI can result in significant and lifelong cognitive, physical, and behavioral deficiencies that require long-term access to health care and disability services.
source: With increases in survival rate following initial injury, TBI can result in significant and lifelong cognitive, physical, and behavioral deficiencies that require long-term access to health care and disability services (LoBue et al., 2019; Pavlovic et al., 2019; Tagliaferri et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TBI is one of the most powerful environmental risk factors associated with the later development of dementia, particularly Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases.
source: It is now understood that TBI represents a process activated at the time of induction, rather than a single event, and whether clinically manifested or asymptomatic, is one of the most powerful environmental risk factors associated with the later development of dementia, and particularly Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases (Barnes et al., 2014; Gardner and Yaffe, 2015; LoBue et al., 2019), triggered by gene changes in pathways that lead to these disorders (Tweedie et al., 2013a; Tweedie et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TBI is triggered by gene changes in pathways that lead to neurodegenerative disorders.
source: It is now understood that TBI represents a process activated at the time of induction, rather than a single event, and whether clinically manifested or asymptomatic, is one of the most powerful environmental risk factors associated with the later development of dementia, and particularly Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases (Barnes et al., 2014; Gardner and Yaffe, 2015; LoBue et al., 2019), triggered by gene changes in pathways that lead to these disorders (Tweedie et al., 2013a; Tweedie et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The incidence of TBI is on the rise.
source: The incidence of TBI is on the rise (Coronado et al., 2015) and by 2020, TBI will comprise the third largest portion of the global disease burden (Hyder et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: By 2020, TBI will comprise the third largest portion of the global disease burden.
source: The incidence of TBI is on the rise (Coronado et al., 2015) and by 2020, TBI will comprise the third largest portion of the global disease burden (Hyder et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TBI-associated brain damage comprises an initial primary damage phase that occurs at the moment of insult.
source: TBI-associated brain damage is often classified into two key stages. An initial primary damage phase occurs at the moment of insult, comprising contusion and laceration, diffuse axonal injury and intracranial hemorrhage that, combined, induce immediate (necrotic) cell death (Greig et al., 2014; LaPlaca et al., 2007) that is difficult to reverse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The primary damage phase of TBI comprises contusion and laceration, diffuse axonal injury and intracranial hemorrhage that induce immediate necrotic cell death.
source: An initial primary damage phase occurs at the moment of insult, comprising contusion and laceration, diffuse axonal injury and intracranial hemorrhage that, combined, induce immediate (necrotic) cell death (Greig et al., 2014; LaPlaca et al., 2007) that is difficult to reverse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The primary damage phase of TBI is difficult to reverse.
source: An initial primary damage phase occurs at the moment of insult, comprising contusion and laceration, diffuse axonal injury and intracranial hemorrhage that, combined, induce immediate (necrotic) cell death (Greig et al., 2014; LaPlaca et al., 2007) that is difficult to reverse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: TBI is followed by a protracted secondary phase that encompasses biological cascades associated with neuroinflammation, ischemia, glutamate excitotoxicity, astrocyte reactivity, and ultimately neuronal dysfunction and apoptosis.
source: This is followed by a protracted secondary phase that encompasses biological cascades associated with neuroinflammation, ischemia, glutamate excitotoxicity, astrocyte reactivity, and ultimately neuronal dysfunction and apoptosis (Barkhoudarian et al., 2011; Greve and Zink, 2009; Morganti-Kossmann et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The secondary phase processes of TBI represent targets for potential drug intervention.
source: These processes represent targets for potential drug intervention (Diaz-Arrastia et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The initiation of an inflammatory response is essential for launching homeostatic neuro-reparative mechanisms following a TBI.
source: The initiation of an inflammatory response is essential for launching homeostatic neuro-reparative mechanisms following a TBI (McCoy and Tansey, 2008; Mckee and Daneshvar, 2015; Schmidt et al., 2005; Sullivan et al., 1999), but if excessive or time-dependently unregulated, these same processes can heighten neuronal dysfunction and degeneration by inducing a self-propagating pathological inflammatory cascade (Frankola et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: If excessive or time-dependently unregulated, inflammatory processes can heighten neuronal dysfunction and degeneration by inducing a self-propagating pathological inflammatory cascade.
source: The initiation of an inflammatory response is essential for launching homeostatic neuro-reparative mechanisms following a TBI (McCoy and Tansey, 2008; Mckee and Daneshvar, 2015; Schmidt et al., 2005; Sullivan et al., 1999), but if excessive or time-dependently unregulated, these same processes can heighten neuronal dysfunction and degeneration by inducing a self-propagating pathological inflammatory cascade (Frankola et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Brain mRNA and protein levels of TNF-α are markedly elevated shortly after TBI in humans.
source: Brain mRNA and protein levels of TNF-α are markedly elevated shortly after TBI in humans (Frugier et al., 2010), and are likewise raised in rodent TBI models.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TNF-α levels are raised in rodent TBI models.
source: Brain mRNA and protein levels of TNF-α are markedly elevated shortly after TBI in humans (Frugier et al., 2010), and are likewise raised in rodent TBI models.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The increase in TNF-α precedes and provokes the generation of multiple other inflammatory cytokines.
source: This increase precedes and provokes the generation of multiple other inflammatory cytokines (Baratz et al., 2015; Lu, 2009; Shohami et al., 1997; Tuttolomondo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TNF-α can intensify oxidative stress, contribute to glutamate release, and exacerbate blood-brain barrier dysfunction, each of which may promote neuronal dysfunction and loss.
source: Depending on its concentration, time of release and signaling pathway engaged, TNF-α can, on the one hand, intensify oxidative stress, contribute to glutamate release, and exacerbate blood-brain barrier dysfunction, each of which may promote neuronal dysfunction and loss (Frankola et al., 2011; McCoy and Tansey, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A delayed, smaller TNF-α rise may augment recovery following TBI by reducing oxidative stress and promoting neurotrophic factor synthesis.
source: On the other hand, a delayed, smaller TNF-α rise may augment recovery following TBI, in line with its purported neuroprotective functions, by reducing oxidative stress and promoting neurotrophic factor synthesis (Patterson and Holahan, 2012; Scherbel et al., 1999; Sullivan et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pomalidomide is an immunomodulatory amino-thalidomide analog that potently inhibits TNF-α synthesis.
source: We recently demonstrated that pomalidomide (Pom), an immunomodulatory amino-thalidomide analog that potently inhibits TNF-α synthesis and which is approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma (Shortt et al., 2013; Terpos et al., 2013), mitigates neuronal loss, neuroinflammation, and behavioral impairments induced by controlled cortical impact (CCI) TBI in rats (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pomalidomide is approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma.
source: We recently demonstrated that pomalidomide (Pom), an immunomodulatory amino-thalidomide analog that potently inhibits TNF-α synthesis and which is approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma (Shortt et al., 2013; Terpos et al., 2013), mitigates neuronal loss, neuroinflammation, and behavioral impairments induced by controlled cortical impact (CCI) TBI in rats (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pomalidomide mitigates neuronal loss, neuroinflammation, and behavioral impairments induced by controlled cortical impact TBI in rats.
source: We recently demonstrated that pomalidomide (Pom), an immunomodulatory amino-thalidomide analog that potently inhibits TNF-α synthesis and which is approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma (Shortt et al., 2013; Terpos et al., 2013), mitigates neuronal loss, neuroinflammation, and behavioral impairments induced by controlled cortical impact (CCI) TBI in rats (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: DP possesses a similar TNF-α lowering action as Pom in RAW 264.7 cellular studies.
source: We find DP possesses a similar TNF-α lowering action as Pom in RAW 264.7 cellular studies, and in rodents challenged with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), but additionally lowers inflammation-induced COX-2 and iNOS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RAW 264.7 cell studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: DP possesses a similar TNF-α lowering action as Pom in rodents challenged with lipopolysaccharide.
source: We find DP possesses a similar TNF-α lowering action as Pom in RAW 264.7 cellular studies, and in rodents challenged with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), but additionally lowers inflammation-induced COX-2 and iNOS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LPS-challenged rats presented in the manuscript.

claim: DP additionally lowers inflammation-induced COX-2 and iNOS compared to Pom.
source: We find DP possesses a similar TNF-α lowering action as Pom in RAW 264.7 cellular studies, and in rodents challenged with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), but additionally lowers inflammation-induced COX-2 and iNOS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cellular and animal studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: DP demonstrated greater potency and efficacy than Pom in rats challenged with CCI TBI with respect to contusion volume, neuronal cell death and functional outcome.
source: This broader activity translated to a more potent activity and efficacy, as compared to Pom, in rats challenged with CCI TBI with respect to contusion volume, neuronal cell death and functional outcome evaluated across a broad variety of behavioral, cellular and molecular indices.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data across multiple measures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of animals with LPS markedly elevated levels of TNF-α in plasma and brain tissues.
source: Treatment of animals with LPS markedly elevated levels of TNF-α. Pretreatment of the animals with Pom and DP significantly reduced these LPS-induced TNF-α increases across plasma and brain tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pretreatment of animals with Pom and DP significantly reduced LPS-induced TNF-α increases across plasma and brain tissues.
source: Treatment of animals with LPS markedly elevated levels of TNF-α. Pretreatment of the animals with Pom and DP significantly reduced these LPS-induced TNF-α increases across plasma and brain tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LPS elevated plasma TNF-α levels by 116.5 ± 6-fold.
source: Specifically, LPS elevated plasma, brain hippocampal and cortex levels by 116.5 ± 6, 11.0 ± 1.6 and 12.0 ± 1.5-fold, respectively (for each, p<0.5 vs. control (veh) without LPS).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LPS-challenged rats.

claim: LPS elevated brain hippocampal TNF-α levels by 11.0 ± 1.6-fold.
source: Specifically, LPS elevated plasma, brain hippocampal and cortex levels by 116.5 ± 6, 11.0 ± 1.6 and 12.0 ± 1.5-fold, respectively (for each, p<0.5 vs. control (veh) without LPS).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LPS-challenged rats.

claim: LPS elevated brain cortex TNF-α levels by 12.0 ± 1.5-fold.
source: Specifically, LPS elevated plasma, brain hippocampal and cortex levels by 116.5 ± 6, 11.0 ± 1.6 and 12.0 ± 1.5-fold, respectively (for each, p<0.5 vs. control (veh) without LPS).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LPS-challenged rats.

claim: DP inhibited LPS-induced TNF-α elevation by 49.3% in plasma, 55.6% in cerebral cortex, and 50.9% in hippocampus.
source: DP inhibited this by 49.3%, 55.6% and 50.9% in plasma, cerebral cortex and hippocampus (p<0.05 vs. LPS alone for each tissue).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LPS-challenged rats treated with DP.

claim: Pom inhibited LPS-induced TNF-α elevation by 57.6% in plasma, 53.9% in cerebral cortex, and 58.5% in hippocampus.
source: Pom provided 57.6%, 53.9% and 58.5% inhibition (p<0.05 vs. LPS alone for each tissue); there was no significant difference between DP and Pom, (Figure 1B left to right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LPS-challenged rats treated with Pom.

claim: There was no significant difference between DP and Pom in inhibiting LPS-induced TNF-α elevation.
source: Pom provided 57.6%, 53.9% and 58.5% inhibition (p<0.05 vs. LPS alone for each tissue); there was no significant difference between DP and Pom, (Figure 1B left to right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Following 21 days of daily administration there were no adverse effects of DP and Pom on animal body weights.
source: Following 21 days of daily administration there were no adverse effects of agents on animal body weights; animals appeared well groomed and were indistinguishable from one another.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DP and Pom were well tolerated at the doses evaluated in the study.
source: DP and Pom (Figure 1A) were well tolerated at the doses evaluated in the present study, 29.5 and 26.4 mg/kg, intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection, respectively: (equimolar to 25 mg/kg thalidomide) in mice and LPS treated rats, and 0.1–0.5 mg/kg intravenous (i.v.) injection in TBI rats, with treated animals being indistinguishable from untreated littermates in relation to a series of assessments focused on health and well-being, as described in Baratz et al., 2015.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of animal health and well-being.

claim: DP possessed a brain/plasma ratio of 0.80 ± 0.08.
source: DP and Pom were quantified by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometric (LC/MS/MS) detection; DP and Pom possessed a brain/plasma ratio of 0.80 ± 0.08 and 0.81 ± 0.04, respectively; indicating that both compounds similarly readily enter the brain following their systemic administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC/MS/MS quantification data.

claim: Pom possessed a brain/plasma ratio of 0.81 ± 0.04.
source: DP and Pom were quantified by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometric (LC/MS/MS) detection; DP and Pom possessed a brain/plasma ratio of 0.80 ± 0.08 and 0.81 ± 0.04, respectively; indicating that both compounds similarly readily enter the brain following their systemic administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC/MS/MS quantification data.

claim: Both DP and Pom similarly readily enter the brain following their systemic administration.
source: DP and Pom were quantified by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometric (LC/MS/MS) detection; DP and Pom possessed a brain/plasma ratio of 0.80 ± 0.08 and 0.81 ± 0.04, respectively; indicating that both compounds similarly readily enter the brain following their systemic administration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar brain/plasma ratios of the two compounds.

claim: DP administered at 5 hr post TBI significantly reduced the contralateral swing ratio from 99.0 ± 1.00% to 66.0 ± 2.92%.
source: DP administered at 5 hr, but not 7 hr, post TBI significantly reduced this ratio from 99.0 ± 1.00% to 66.0 ± 2.92% (p<0.001), with a value of 50% representing that found in normal healthy animals (Borlongan and Sanberg, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by EBST behavioral test data.

claim: DP administered at 7 hr post TBI did not significantly reduce the contralateral swing ratio.
source: DP administered at 5 hr, but not 7 hr, post TBI significantly reduced this ratio from 99.0 ± 1.00% to 66.0 ± 2.92% (p<0.001), with a value of 50% representing that found in normal healthy animals (Borlongan and Sanberg, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by EBST behavioral test data.

claim: TBI + DP animals showed significantly better beam walking performance vs. TBI + Veh treated animals (12.95 ± 0.87 vs. 59.0 ± 1.00 s).
source: In contrast, TBI + DP animals showed significantly better beam walking performance vs. TBI + Veh treated animals (12.95 ± 0.87 vs. 59.0 ± 1.00 s, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by beam walking test data.

claim: DP significantly mitigated TBI-induced neurological functional deficits with improvement at 5 hr being greater than at 7 hr after TBI.
source: DP significantly mitigated this deficit with improvement at 5 hr being greater than at 7 hr after TBI (p<0.001 vs. p<0.01; Figure 2C (iii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by mNSS score data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Post treatment with DP at 5 hr, but not 7 hr, mitigated TBI-induced impairment in fine sensorimotor coordination.
source: Finally, a TBI-induced deficit in fine sensorimotor coordination was evident by delayed time for adhesive-removal, as evaluated by a tactile test (Figure 2C (iv); 152.4 ± 3.91 vs. 12.6 ± 0.97 s for TBI + Veh vs. sham, respectively, p<0.001). Post treatment with DP at 5 hr, but not 7 hr, likewise mitigated this impairment.
evidence: This claim is supported by tactile adhesive removal test data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DP (0.5 mg/kg) administered at 5 hr after TBI induced a significant reduction in contusion volume relative to the TBI + Veh group.
source: Intravenous administration of DP (0.5 mg/kg) at 5 hr but not at 7 hr after TBI induced a significant reduction in contusion volume relative to the TBI + Veh group.
evidence: This claim is supported by contusion volume data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DP (0.5 mg/kg) administered at 7 hr after TBI did not induce a significant reduction in contusion volume relative to the TBI + Veh group.
source: Intravenous administration of DP (0.5 mg/kg) at 5 hr but not at 7 hr after TBI induced a significant reduction in contusion volume relative to the TBI + Veh group.
evidence: This claim is supported by contusion volume data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DP 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg reduced the TBI-induced contusion volume to 12.9 ± 0.22% and 7.4 ± 0.87%, respectively.
source: The loss of cortical tissue evident in TBI + Veh animals (19.0 ± 0.74% of the contralateral hemisphere volume (Figure 3B)) was significantly mitigated by DP 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg, reducing the contusion volume to 12.9 ± 0.22% and 7.4 ± 0.87%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by contusion volume quantification data.

claim: DP 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg represent a 32% and 61% reduction in contusion volume compared to TBI+Veh animals.
source: This represents a 32% and 61% reduction compared to TBI+Veh animals (both p<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by contusion volume quantification data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pom 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg reduced the TBI-induced contusion volume to 14.2 ± 0.93% and 11.6 ± 1.02% of the contralateral hemisphere volume.
source: In contrast, Pom 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg reduced the injury volume to 14.2 ± 0.93% and 11.6 ± 1.02% of the contralateral hemisphere volume, representing a 25% and 39% reduction compared to the TBI + Veh group (p<0.01 and p<0.001; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by contusion volume quantification data.

claim: Pom 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg represent a 25% and 39% reduction in contusion volume compared to the TBI + Veh group.
source: In contrast, Pom 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg reduced the injury volume to 14.2 ± 0.93% and 11.6 ± 1.02% of the contralateral hemisphere volume, representing a 25% and 39% reduction compared to the TBI + Veh group (p<0.01 and p<0.001; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by contusion volume quantification data.

claim: Pom-mediated protection was significantly less than that achieved by the same dose of DP.
source: This Pom-mediated protection was thus significantly less than that achieved by the same dose of DP (p<0.05; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative contusion volume data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TBI + Veh-treated animals demonstrated substantial cerebral cortex and hippocampal tissue damage ipsilateral to injury at 24 hr and 7 days following CCI.
source: As illustrated in the top two images of Figure 3C, TBI +Veh-treated animals demonstrated substantial cerebral cortex and hippocampal tissue damage ipsilateral to injury, as evidenced by hyperintensity abnormalities at 24 hr and 7 days following CCI, with the later time showing a greater area of injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A single administration of either dose of DP (0.1 or 0.5 mg/kg) at 5 hr post TBI resulted in a comparatively smaller injury volume of hyperintensity and associated damage.
source: In contrast, a single administration of either dose of DP (0.1 or 0.5 mg/kg) at 5 hr post TBI (Figure 3C center and lower panels) resulted in a comparatively smaller injury volume of hyperintensity and associated damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DP and Pom were without behavioral activity when administered to Sham animals.
source: Illustrated in Figure 3D, DP and Pom were without behavioral activity when administered to Sham animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Post-treatment with DP (0.1 mg/kg and 0.5 mg/kg) or Pom (0.5 mg/kg) at 5 hr after TBI improved outcomes across all measured behavioral outcomes.
source: However, post-treatment with DP (0.1 mg/kg and 0.5 mg/kg) or Pom (0.5 mg/kg) at 5 hr after TBI improved outcomes across all measured behavioral outcomes (neurological function, asymmetrical motor behavior, sensorimotor function and motor coordination (Figure 3E (i) – (iv)).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DP (0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg) demonstrated similar or significantly superior efficacy compared to Pom (0.5 mg/kg) across all behavioral tests.
source: Notably, DP (0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg) demonstrated similar or significantly superior efficacy compared to Pom (0.5 mg/kg) across all behavioral tests (p<0.01 and 0.001), and Pom 0.1 mg/kg lacked significant activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative behavioral test data.

claim: Pom 0.1 mg/kg lacked significant activity in behavioral tests.
source: Notably, DP (0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg) demonstrated similar or significantly superior efficacy compared to Pom (0.5 mg/kg) across all behavioral tests (p<0.01 and 0.001), and Pom 0.1 mg/kg lacked significant activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data.

claim: The NeuN-positive cell number was significantly decreased in the cortical contusion margin of TBI + Veh vs. sham animals (238.20 ± 11.45 cells/mm2 vs. 649.74 ± 43.00 cells/mm2).
source: Utilizing an antibody against the neuronal marker NeuN to label neurons, the NeuN-positive (+) cell number was found to be significantly decreased in the cortical contusion margin of TBI + Veh vs. sham animals (238.20 ± 11.45 cells/mm2 vs. 649.74 ± 43.00 cells/mm2, p<0.001; Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by NeuN immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Treatment with DP (0.5 mg/kg) markedly attenuated TBI-induced neuronal loss to 523.31 ± 20.40 cells/mm2.
source: Treatment with DP (0.5 mg/kg) or Pom (0.5 mg/kg) markedly attenuated this neuronal loss to 523.31 ± 20.40 cells/mm2 and 423.93 ± 46.68 cells/mm2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by NeuN immunohistochemistry quantification data.

claim: Treatment with Pom (0.5 mg/kg) markedly attenuated TBI-induced neuronal loss to 423.93 ± 46.68 cells/mm2.
source: Treatment with DP (0.5 mg/kg) or Pom (0.5 mg/kg) markedly attenuated this neuronal loss to 523.31 ± 20.40 cells/mm2 and 423.93 ± 46.68 cells/mm2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by NeuN immunohistochemistry quantification data.

claim: DP (0.5 mg/kg) represents a mitigation of TBI-induced neuronal loss of 69.2% vs. the TBI + Veh group.
source: This represents a mitigation of TBI-induced neuronal loss of 69.2% and 45.1%, respectively, vs. the TBI + Veh group (p<0.001 and p<0.001; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by NeuN immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pom (0.5 mg/kg) represents a mitigation of TBI-induced neuronal loss of 45.1% vs. the TBI + Veh group.
source: This represents a mitigation of TBI-induced neuronal loss of 69.2% and 45.1%, respectively, vs. the TBI + Veh group (p<0.001 and p<0.001; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by NeuN immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The aberrant overexpression of α-synuclein coincident with neuroinflammation in brain following TBI suggests α-synuclein as a key pathological link between TBI and later development of PD-like symptoms.
source: In the light of studies demonstrating the aberrant overexpression of α-synuclein coincident with neuroinflammation in brain following TBI, and suggesting α-synuclein as key a pathological link between TBI and later development of PD-like symptoms in humans and animal models of TBI (Acosta et al., 2015; Wong and Hazrati, 2013), we evaluated whether DP and Pom could mitigate α-synuclein-induced toxicity in primary neuronal cultures containing dopaminergic neurons.
